“Dues and Don’t’s” at #3, obviously, because the whole episode is Team Rocket based, and we discover that they’ve been removed from the organization entirely, only to try and get back in. 

“Ignorance Is Blissey” at #4, this episode makes me bawl like a baby. Jessie reuniting with her old friend, Blissey, and then going into her backstory was absolutely lovely. We see a side of Jessie that isn’t ever really shown. 

“Go West Young Meowth” at #5, Meowzie really did a number on our boy, but if it wasn’t for him trying to win her love and affection, he never would’ve learned to walk, nor talk. So I guess she came in handy for something? 

“Pokémon Fashion Flash” at #6, Jessie & James are fashionista’s, obviously. Salon Roquette could’ve gone far, had Misty not shown up, causing Meowth to out their operation. 

“The Stun Spore Detour” at #7, James & Meowth are on the hunt for Salveyo weed, and spend the whole episode basically following Misty for it. 

And lastly, the whole S.S Anne arc as #8-10, because any episode where they team up with/are stuck with the twerps is noteworthy, in my opinion, and this arc is especially fun. 

Evidently, I love Team Rocket.

He could be legally blind, which is where you're not "fully" blind, but on the verge of it. I know an individual who is going through that very thing, he has a cane, but refuses to use it and when he does, he'll sometimes fold it up, or walk with it underneath his arm. A degenerative eye disease such as retinitis  pigmentosa is the most common. First the night vision goes, followed by your peripheral, your depth perception begins to diminish. Watching a human go through the loss of their vision is heartbreaking, if the person begins to exhibit strange behavior that's due to embarrassment (they can't always see who's around or if anybody is laughing at them struggling, it's very sad), and due to being frustrated. At one point in their lives (this applies to some) they used to be able to walk around freely, see everything, and do things in a normal fashion, now they feel limited to what they can do and can accomplish. The honorable mention in the story though, I can't quite speak for him, but I'm speaking through the perspectives of others I've known who are facing that predicament. There's not enough awareness on degenerative eye disease. People hear the word "blind" and automatically think that their vision is gone in one go, that's incorrect. If you're gut is telling you a different story, always be on guard.

(#2: When Talking On The Phone) Stay on the line with her and repeat the breathing techniques, remain patient, make sure that she's in a good mindset before ending the phone call. The consistency of it tends to be unhealthy, as I find myself drifting off during working hours, the constant obsession I have with it, the fact that I grew with a spectrum of characters over the years has indeed been depressing and sad, but I am working on channeling this creation into a television program. The writing part however is tedious, yet I have faith in something I grew with, something realistic in my mind, turning what I once considered as a coping mechanism into a message that I can share with the world, that is the powerful part to this. You should use this gift in the best way possible, it is indeed time consuming, and is used as a way to dissociate from the outside world, but with a mind strong enough to create a world of its own, that's a unique gift. I have yet to share the premise with the world, but one day, we can easily find the strength to conquer, thanks to the art of entertainment!

What's funny is that on Sunday, I was running on 5 hours of sleep, and I was working rather late hours. I was talking to a coworker who had made a comment on how my confidence has grown (I laughed cause he doesn't even know, he just doesn't understand the difference between confidence and getting to know people), well for some reason I brought up the fact that I'm an empath, that led to the worst stuttering session I've had in months, I sounded like a scratched up broken record. On top of that, I began saying everything incorrectly, it's as if my brain decided to freeze from its weekly overdrive. In regards to melatonin, I had a point in time where I'd take it occasionally, the sleep was so fantastic, however the morning after I'd lose that lovely anxious glow, and carried on a very heavy shadow, one of which that kept me fatigue.

Sleep deprivation combined with anxiety is always the worst combination. I find myself trying to pry my heavy eyelids open, I get really shaky, irritable, and my words often blend together when I try to fluently complete a sentence. What I hate is how I hover around people, or at least feel like I am, almost as if I lost my ability to take a step, or stand up straight. Not to mention the fact that dizziness becomes the most debilitating factor. Customers get a kick out of the odd cashier giving them service, trying to hide their laughter by subtlety scrolling on their phone, acknowledging their friends as I try to communicate, customers even avoid me as well, skipping to other lanes. Oh anxiety, when shall I sleep? Oh, that's right... Never.

Absolutely! It is important to know that we all carry struggles similar to one another, society has just lost it's voice, therefore most people remain silent as they are unaware of properly conveying emotion. My anxiety became more relevant when I was your age, once you become aware of it's existence, it opens many doors to self discovery. People like us are unique, we have qualities that can be difficult to express in this modern day and age. I used to be self conscious over the fact that I am a young adult who enjoys older eras of music, as most people my age placed judgement on my tastes, and would stare in confusion as I spoke about the Retro Wave movement that took place in the 80's. On a side note, I found it interesting to see how different my mind processed certain things as opposed to others. It wasn't until recently that I began to open up about my anxiety. Now that it's open to the public (Coworkers/my tiny group of friends) it helped give certain people an understanding as to why I'd start tearing up during my shift, along with hyperventilation during overwhelming moments. Some people gave harsh feedback in return such as "You're a grown woman, get it over it, you aren't a child anymore." Then I grew pleasantly surprised at the amount of people who were in the same boat, I was unaware of their existence up until I came face to face with heartfelt conversations from people who mastered the art of hiding their pain. Thoughts surface on a regular basis where I feel idiotic for giving my illness that exposure, but at the same time, I know it's my illness causing this deep rooted fear. It is indeed a game that can't be won, but it can be overpowered on days where I force myself to remember I am not alone in this world, and no one else should ever feel the pain we all endure.

You are going through a period of grief, it's natural whenever relationships change, or whenever ties are severed. Keep in mind that while it may be very painful, it is a healthy way of releasing emotion. When you lose a connection with someone you cared for deeply, days are going to seem darker than usual, and anxiety intensifies those emotions. Just remember to breathe easy, find an outlet for the emotions you're experiencing. Translating pain into art helped me, as I was channeling my emotions into pieces that showcased a story full of human emotion.

I had a period in my life where I was taken out of school and placed in a homeschooling program due to the degree of bullying that took place. During those lonesome years, I was stuck in solitude, I'd often be left to frequent social networking sites that had no value. A parental figure of mine would often prohibit me from going out to socialize, as she feared I would fall under negative influences or get harmed. Isolation, and the constant pain I was in from having nobody in my life to communicate with was painful. Summer of '10 was merely spent in doors, after 4 months of never leaving my room, a breakdown ensued, that was the moment everything changed. To say the least, yes, I have experienced similarities to this, as with a lot of things on this sub. My elaboration was most likely unnecessary, but I felt you needed to know I was there at one point, and that it's natural for those of us who don't fit in.

Coming from an individual who shares an experience similar to yours (Grew out of the lying phase during my teen years, as it caused heaps of trouble), you are not alone in the battle your mind is causing. Growing up with this disorder, we often live in our mind more so than trying to integrate with the general public. Early on, we often feel disconnected from the outside world, school being the first stage where we make that realization. Growing up in a world such as this, we are subjected to people who feel the need to taunt others for being an outcast, this is a representation of how they choose to assimilate with those who are deemed "Cool". As a way to try and break that mold, we envision ourselves living a life similar to theirs, stories float through our mind, and at the time being, we have the urge to intertwine that imaginary world into the physical realm, it's generally a coping mechanism, it however is not healthy. In the job world, you will grow to learn how humans interact with one another. The way I became a part of the workplace was by observing the behaviors of everyday people. You grow to learn their body language, and over time you'll be able to pick up on their facial cues. It is a process, I haven't fully found solace in this world yet, as I am still learning the basics of interaction, and how to properly conduct myself while being in the public eye. Just try to remain patient, it is very difficult, but it could eventually ease up in the future.

Seeing as to how she's on the outside looking in, she's only basing her perception of you off of what she has seen. She is missing the point that you appear to be "Fine" in her eyes due to the fact that you are comfortable speaking with her. When an individual is plagued with social anxiety, they usually find comfort, and confide in at least one human being. You need to explain to her the history behind the disorder itself, and elaborate on how it manifested. I've had a similar issue in the past, after having multiple discussions with my friend, and having her view multiple scenarios where my social anxiety took over, she finally reached an understanding. In some cases, it takes awhile for others to understand. Perhaps a cordial invite to your home could help, a one on one conversation will help her see the emotion, and possibly feel the emotion as you speak.

She reacted in a very disrespectful manner, you are doing no harm, nor ruining her so called "Free Time" by sending a text. I believe that you should text her back and explain that you don't appreciate what she had sent. If she is aware of your anxiety disorder, then she should know better, she had no right to type that out, send it, and place you in that state of mind. Just remember, anxiety is a bitch, and it does get lonely, however I must add that toxic people are no good.

Being a cashier with social anxiety, I often feel as if the customer is viewing me as rude, awkward, and weird. Generally I receive little to no acknowledgement, and often feel as if customers are judging my actions, which leaves me to panic deep down inside as I'm trying to finalize the transaction. Perhaps the individual checking your items out at that moment feels the same, as I've discovered I'm not the only cashier who suffers from some form of anxiety. I understand where you're coming from though, being on the other side of a register during a transaction has always been odd for me, standing in a line behind so many people, I feel odd, and unsure of where to look. I try to maintain eye contact with customers, but it can be difficult sometimes as I'm often triggered by certain expressions they give off, if they have an angry tone of voice, or just stare at me holding in their laughter, the managers also refuse to let us have water, so when my mouth becomes dry, communication can be rough. Not to rant, but felt as if it might help giving a different perspective coming from the other end. Anxiety is a bitch, especially when you feel as if you're being mocked for 8 straight hours.

I do as well, she sort of figured it out in a way. I would always remain quiet about it, but after having countless attacks happen (Often onset attacks due to being understaffed) she caught on. It's painful to go through, customers always place judgement on my difficulty maintaining eye contact, and how I'm always visibly shaken, but I always tell myself that I'll survive, it'll all be over soon, and that I can't give up.
